li.a: South China Morning Post, 24 April 2026: Inside 14k, how a Hong Kong triad grew into a global crime syndicate
South China Morning Post, 4 February 2017: A brief history of Hong Kong's triad gangs
The Standard, 13 September 2021: Triad road chase ends in police station smash
The Globe and Mail, 18 February 2013: Wiretap connects alleged Asian gang leader to triad violence that spilled into Vancouver
Asia Times, 10 December 2020: US sanctions China crime godfather 'Broken Tooth'
OCCRP: Myanmar military raids scam center, detains over 2,000 suspects

content.p: The 14K is a Hong Kong triad society whose name is an exception among the well-established triads, most of which have auspicious names. Sun Yee On means roughly "new, righteousness, peace", and Wo Shing Wo stands for "peace, victory, unity". The 14K's name has no agreed meaning. Its origin is the subject of several legends, and police and reporters have linked its members to drug trafficking, while in recent years the group has been accused of involvement in online fraud compounds in Myanmar.

The South China Morning Post, drawing on the Australian criminologist Henry Prunckun, places the group's beginnings at a Canton address on Po Wah Road, where Kuomintang general Kot Siu-wong is said to have set it up. The paper dates the seeds of the group to 1945, when Kot gathered men to fight the advancing army of Mao Zedong. When the Communist Party won the civil war in 1949, many of Kot's operatives moved to British Hong Kong and took the name 14K. Prunckun called it "the last triad society to be formed on mainland China", and said it was modelled on "an honourable military association".

The explanation of the name is disputed. The South China Morning Post reports that some say the "K" stands for Kot, others for the Kuomintang, and others for Kiu Kiang Street in Kowloon, where the group was established in Hong Kong. The name could also refer to 14-karat gold, a symbol of strength. The paper's own summary is that the origin of the name is one of the group's several legends.

Kot died in 1953. According to the same account, the men he had gathered allegedly began to take part in crime, including opium production in Myanmar and drug dealing between Hong Kong, Taiwan and Southeast Asia. Sub-factions grew in the meantime. The paper cites William P. Morgan's 1960 book, Triad Societies in Hong Kong, which put the group at about 80,000 members in the 1950s, with control over districts from Sham Shui Po and Kowloon City to Tsuen Wan and the New Territories' east side.

In 1956, the group was involved in the riots that followed tensions between pro-Kuomintang and pro-Communist factions. The South China Morning Post says it was reported that the 14K joined forces with Wo On Lok, also known as Shui Fong, and pushed the protests into serious violence. The paper counts the aftermath as roughly 6,000 people arrested, about 500 hurt and 59 dead, among them the spouse of a Swiss official. The colonial government then set up a Triad Societies Bureau, later renamed the Organised Crime and Triad Bureau, which raided the groups. The paper says the raids did not stop the criminal activity.
content.h2: The Walled City and the street
content.p: Between the 1950s and the 1970s, the Kowloon Walled City, which housed about 30,000 people, was largely controlled by Sun Yee On and the 14K, according to the South China Morning Post's 2017 history of the city's triads. The British government followed a hands-off policy towards the enclave, and it became a centre of crime and poor sanitation. The British and Chinese governments agreed in January 1987 to demolish it. Work began in 1993 and was completed the following year, and the site is now a park.

The same 2017 article lists the Sun Yee On, the 14K and Wo Shing Wo as the leading triads of the time, and describes the rivalries between them as common. It says prospective members take "36 oaths" during initiation, and that gangs have often tried to extort local tradesmen and workers. The 2026 series in the same paper adds that in the 1970s a youth gang associated with the 14K in the Tsz Wan Shan estate became notorious around the Walled City.

The 14K's trade in narcotics is where the group's reach is most often described. The South China Morning Post, citing a 2003 paper published by the US Library of Congress, says Dutch police believed the 14K had monopolised the import of heroin into Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg through Bangkok from 1987. The same article says the group was reported to control half of the British narcotics market, through trafficking networks that also reached Turkey, Kosovo and Colombia. The paper does not say who made the UK claim.

In 1997, Japan's National Police Agency said the 14K, together with other Hong Kong gangs, had been expanding into Japan since the 1980s and was working with yakuza groups to bring illegal Chinese migrants into the country. In 2000, Thai police seized more than 100 kilograms of heroin on its way to the United States and linked the seizure to the 14K. The 2003 paper also lists Australia, Austria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Philippines, Portugal, Russia, Spain and the United States among the 14K's main areas of activity.
content.h2: Sun Yee On and the Sha Tin chase
content.p: Rivalry with Sun Yee On has produced violence in Hong Kong in recent years. In September 2021, The Standard reported a chase that began with a gambling debt. A 26-year-old waiter owed HK$60,000 to the Sun Yee On society. According to the paper, a 27-year-old Sun Yee On member and three associates clubbed him in Sha Tin. A friend of the waiter, a 14K member aged 36, stepped in and was also attacked. He then used WhatsApp to send his associates a GPS location.

The Standard says the Sun Yee On group took both men away in a white minivan. The group then drove to Kowloon Tong to pick up an associate, and 14K members in three cars, tracking the location, intercepted them. The outnumbered group drove off towards Tsuen Wan with the 14K vehicles behind. One 14K car collided with a truck at a junction on Yeung Uk Road. The minivan then drove through a gate at Kwai Chung Police Station and into the car park, while the pursuing cars waited outside.

Police arrested the four Sun Yee On members in the van, along with the 14K man they had taken. Seven others were rounded up later, 12 people in all. Five people were charged, the paper says, with assault, dangerous driving, criminal damage and triad membership, and were granted bail after a hearing at Sha Tin Magistrates' Court. The other seven were released on police bail. The Standard reports that Police Commissioner Raymond Siu Chak-yee then led follow-up raids on gambling dens and clubs in Tsim Sha Tsui, which it says were allegedly controlled by the 14K and Sun Yee On, and that these produced another 115 arrests.

The group's conflicts have also crossed into Canada. The Globe and Mail reported in 2013 on court papers that were to be used in an immigration case against Lai Tong Sang. Police in Macau and Hong Kong, the paper says, considered Lai to be the "dragon head" of the Wo On Lok triad, also called Shui Fong, which was then in a violent turf war with the 14K. Lai was shot at in a drive-by attack on his southwest Vancouver home in 1997, nine months after he entered Canada, and the paper describes the attack as a sign that the Macau triad war had reached Vancouver.

The Canada Border Services Agency's 2011 report, which the Globe and Mail obtained, quoted wiretap evidence gathered by Hong Kong police. The agency wrote: "A 14K Triad member in Hong Kong asked 14K members in Vancouver to murder Lai because of the Shui Fong and 14K dispute in Macau." The newspaper reports that the wiretap also detailed a call in which 14K Triad members decided whether a contract should be put on Lai. The paper also reports that Lai's lawyer, Peter Chapman, said he could not comment because the proceedings were ongoing, and argued that it is not an indictable offence to be part of a secret society or to take part in a turf war. Lai, who is a citizen of Portugal according to the paper, was admitted in 1996 after his application, made through the Los Angeles consulate, was not checked against his history with Canadian officers in Hong Kong. No criminal charge is reported in the article. The hearing was set for February 2013.

The figure most often linked to the group in these pages is Wan Kuok-koi, known as "Broken Tooth". Asia Times reports that he spent 14 years behind bars in Macau for a string of murders and bombings, and was released in 2012. In December 2020, the US Treasury imposed sanctions on him, on the World Hongmen History and Culture Association, based in Cambodia, and on the Hong Kong-based Dongmei Group. Asia Times describes Wan as head of the 14K, and the Treasury said he had built operations in Cambodia, Myanmar and Palau. It described the Hongmen association as a front for crime, involved in cryptocurrencies, real estate, casinos and a security company that works on Belt and Road investments. Treasury said the 14K "is utilizing Broken Tooth's World Hongmen History and Culture Association as an effort to legitimize itself." The sanctions freeze assets under US jurisdiction and bar American people and companies from doing business with the named parties. Asia Times presents these as the Treasury's allegations, and the article does not describe any court finding on them.

The group's most recent prominent case is the KK Park compound on the Myanmar border with Thailand. The South China Morning Post says the 14K has been accused of involvement in the compound, where industrial-scale online fraud, money laundering and human trafficking were said to take place, with reports of torture and unlawful imprisonment. In 2024, the German broadcaster Deutsche Welle reported, based on several sources and escapees, that the guards were from Myanmar but "the bosses of the operation are Chinese". The paper reports that a report by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, issued in April 2025, points to ties between the KK Park network and senior 14K figures, one of them a Macau-based leader sanctioned by the US in 2020. The paper's account of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime report is secondhand here; the report's own text is not quoted here.

OCCRP reports that Myanmar's military raided KK Park and arrested 2,198 people, and seized 30 Starlink satellite receivers, according to state media. The South China Morning Post dates the military raid to late 2025. OCCRP says the compound was allegedly used by international syndicates for money laundering, online fraud and romance and investment scams, and that its construction allegedly began in 2020 and was completed after the 2021 coup, according to the activist group Justice for Myanmar. The United Nations estimate cited by OCCRP puts the sums siphoned from victims in East and Southeast Asia at between $18 billion and $37 billion in a single year. OCCRP also notes that the ruling junta itself has been accused of facilitating the scam industry.

The saved reporting gives no agreed count of 14K members. The South China Morning Post cites Morgan's estimate of 80,000 in the 1950s, and a 2001 mainland Chinese media claim of 200,000 that the paper says remains unproven. Its 2026 article says that in the 2010s many factions split away as leaders changed and old divisions resurfaced, and that efforts to unify the group met resistance. The 2017 history estimates there could be as many as 100,000 triad members in the city, across all the triads.

The reporting cited here covers three kinds of material. The Standard describes a 2021 car chase that began with a gambling debt, with charges that were at the bail stage in its reporting. The Macau prison term of Wan Kuok-koi, as Asia Times describes it, is the only court outcome on the group's leadership in these pages. Everything else, including the US sanctions, the Canadian wiretap claims and the reports on the Myanmar compounds, is an allegation or a government claim, and it is reported here with its source.
